s: Mechanism that propagates overload signals upstream so producers slow down before consumers collapse.
w: When a consumer is overwhelmed (queue full, latency spike), it signals the producer to reduce send rate - via bounded queues blocking publishers, credit-based flow control, or explicit NAK signals. Without backpressure, producers run unbounded causing OOM or cascading failure. Kafka consumer lag, Flink credit-based flow, and TCP windowing are all forms of backpressure.
use: Stream processing pipelines where downstream slowdown must not crash upstream
Database write ingestion where DB commit rate is the hard ceiling
Microservice call chains where one slow service should not cause upstream retries
Message queue consumers that cannot keep up during traffic spikes
avoid: Unbounded buffers between stages - they just delay failure and increase blast radius
Ignoring backpressure signals - if consumer lag grows, something must give

props.buffer_size: Max items queued before producer blocks

pat.d: Circuit breaker stops calls; backpressure throttles them - complementary strategies.

pits: Unbounded buffers masking the real problem - memory grows until OOM kills the process
Backpressure invisible to operators - instrument consumer lag and buffer depth as first-class metrics
tips: TCP itself is the canonical backpressure example: receiver window shrinks when app is slow
Interview answer: backpressure is graceful degradation, not failure prevention
